stem: India is the __________ most populous country in the world.
solution: India is now the WORLD's MOST POPULOUS country, having OVERTAKEN CHINA (India's population has crossed 1.4 billion). India, with about a sixth of humanity, is one of the two demographic giants of the world (the other being China). Its huge population is a central feature of its geography, economy, and development challenges. So India is the most populous country. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The distribution of population in India is __________.
options: Uneven — some states/regions are densely populated (like the northern plains and Kerala) while others are sparsely populated (like deserts, mountains, and forests)
solution: The distribution of POPULATION in INDIA is UNEVEN. Some states and regions are DENSELY POPULATED — especially the fertile NORTHERN PLAINS (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal — India's most populous states) and states like KERALA and parts of the coasts and deltas — while OTHERS are SPARSELY populated — the DESERTS (Rajasthan's Thar), the high MOUNTAINS (Himalayas), and dense FORESTS and rugged areas (parts of the North-East and central India). Favourable conditions (fertile land, water, industry) attract population, while harsh terrain repels it. So India's population is unevenly distributed. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The most populous state in India is __________.
solution: UTTAR PRADESH is the MOST POPULOUS state in India — it has the largest population of any Indian state (well over 200 million people), located in the fertile Ganga plain. (Bihar, Maharashtra, and West Bengal are also among the most populous.) In contrast, SIKKIM has the smallest population among the states, and GOA and the North-Eastern states (like Mizoram) also have small populations. So the most populous state is Uttar Pradesh. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: 'Population density' in India (persons per square kilometre) is highest in states/areas like __________ and lowest in __________.
options: Bihar, West Bengal, Kerala, and the NCT of Delhi (highest); Arunachal Pradesh and desert/mountain areas (lowest)
solution: POPULATION DENSITY (persons per square kilometre) in India is HIGHEST in states/areas with fertile land, good economic opportunities, or high urbanisation — such as BIHAR, WEST BENGAL, KERALA, Uttar Pradesh, and especially the NCT of DELHI (very high density). It is LOWEST in states with harsh terrain and sparse settlement — such as ARUNACHAL PRADESH and other North-Eastern hill states, and the DESERT/MOUNTAIN areas. Density thus reflects the same physical and human factors that shape distribution. So the highest densities are in Bihar/Bengal/Kerala/Delhi, the lowest in Arunachal and desert/mountain areas. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's population has grown rapidly, and the phase of very rapid growth (the 'population explosion') occurred especially after __________.
options: 1921 (called the 'year of the Great Divide', after which population grew steadily and rapidly)
solution: India's population has grown rapidly, and the phase of very rapid growth (the 'POPULATION EXPLOSION') occurred especially AFTER 1921. The year 1921 is called the 'YEAR of the GREAT DIVIDE' in India's demographic history: BEFORE 1921, the population grew slowly and fluctuated (with periods of decline due to famines and epidemics); AFTER 1921, the death rate began to fall (due to better health, food, and control of famines/epidemics) while the birth rate remained high, so the population grew STEADILY and RAPIDLY, decade after decade. So the rapid growth began after 1921. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The main reason for India's rapid population growth in the 20th century was __________.
options: A sharp fall in the death rate (due to better health care, food supply, and control of famines and epidemics), while the birth rate remained high
A rise in the death rate
A fall in the birth rate only
solution: The main REASON for India's RAPID POPULATION GROWTH in the 20th century was a SHARP FALL in the DEATH RATE — brought about by better HEALTH CARE (medicines, vaccines, control of epidemics like plague, cholera, malaria), improved FOOD SUPPLY (agricultural advances reducing famines), and better sanitation — WHILE the BIRTH RATE REMAINED HIGH (traditional attitudes favouring large families changed only slowly). With many more people surviving but births still high, the population grew explosively. (In recent decades, the birth rate has also fallen, slowing growth.) So the cause was falling death rates while birth rates stayed high. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In recent decades, India's population growth RATE has __________.
options: Begun to slow down (decline), as the birth rate has fallen, though the total population is still increasing
Reversed into decline of total population
solution: In RECENT DECADES, India's population GROWTH RATE has BEGUN to SLOW DOWN (decline) — the RATE of increase is falling — because the BIRTH RATE has been FALLING (due to development, education, urbanisation, family planning, and changing lifestyles), moving India through the later stages of the demographic transition. Importantly, this means the TOTAL POPULATION is STILL INCREASING (as births still exceed deaths, and due to population momentum from the large young population), but at a SLOWER rate than before. So the growth rate is slowing, though the total population still rises. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Population composition' in India includes aspects such as __________.
options: Rural-urban composition, age structure, sex ratio, literacy, occupational structure, and linguistic/religious composition
Only the total number of people
solution: POPULATION COMPOSITION in INDIA includes several aspects: the RURAL-URBAN composition (India is still largely rural but rapidly urbanising); the AGE STRUCTURE (India has a large young/working-age population — a potential demographic dividend); the SEX RATIO (females per 1,000 males — historically adverse in India); LITERACY (which has risen but with gaps); the OCCUPATIONAL structure (a large share still in agriculture, but shifting); and the LINGUISTIC and RELIGIOUS composition (India's great diversity of languages and religions). These attributes describe the character of India's population beyond mere numbers. So India's population composition includes rural-urban, age, sex ratio, literacy, occupation, and linguistic/religious aspects. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The sex ratio in India (females per 1,000 males) has historically been __________.
options: Adverse/unfavourable to females (fewer females than males), reflecting gender discrimination, though there is some improvement over time
solution: The SEX RATIO in INDIA (the number of FEMALES per 1,000 MALES) has historically been ADVERSE/UNFAVOURABLE to FEMALES — that is, there are FEWER FEMALES than males (the sex ratio is below 1,000). This reflects deep-rooted GENDER DISCRIMINATION — son preference, neglect of the girl child, sex-selective practices, and higher female mortality in some age groups. It is a serious social concern (the 'missing women' problem). There has been SOME IMPROVEMENT over recent decades, but the ratio remains a matter of worry, especially the low CHILD sex ratio. So India's sex ratio has been adverse to females, with some improvement. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's age structure shows that a large proportion of its population is __________.
options: Young and of working age — giving India a 'demographic dividend' opportunity (a large potential workforce)
solution: India's AGE STRUCTURE shows that a LARGE PROPORTION of its population is YOUNG and of WORKING AGE (a large share is in the 15–59/64 productive age group, and a big youth population). This gives India a 'DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND' OPPORTUNITY — a large potential WORKFORCE that, IF healthy, educated, skilled, and productively employed, can drive rapid economic growth. This youthful age structure (a legacy of past high birth rates) is a major asset, but realising the dividend requires heavy investment in education, health, skills, and job creation. So India has a young, working-age population offering a demographic dividend. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The majority of India's population still lives in __________, though urbanisation is increasing.
solution: The MAJORITY of India's population still lives in RURAL AREAS (VILLAGES) — India remains a predominantly rural country, with a large share of its people engaged in or dependent on agriculture and rural livelihoods. However, URBANISATION is INCREASING rapidly: the urban population and the number and size of cities are growing steadily (through rural-to-urban migration and city growth), and the urban share is rising over time. So while most Indians are still rural, the country is urbanising. So the majority live in rural areas, though urbanisation is rising. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): India faces the challenge of a large and growing population. Reason (R): A large population puts pressure on resources, food, jobs, services, and the environment, requiring careful planning and development. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India FACES the CHALLENGE of a LARGE and GROWING POPULATION. And the reason is (R) that a large population puts PRESSURE on RESOURCES (land, water, energy), FOOD supply, JOBS/employment, public SERVICES (education, health, housing, sanitation), and the ENVIRONMENT — requiring CAREFUL PLANNING and DEVELOPMENT to provide for everyone and ensure sustainability. Because so many people must be fed, employed, housed, and served (and the environment protected), managing the population is a major developmental challenge (A). (A large young population is also a potential asset if well utilised.) So R correctly explains A.

stem: Literacy in India has __________.
options: Increased significantly over the decades, though gaps remain (e.g., between males and females, and between states/regions)
solution: LITERACY in INDIA has INCREASED SIGNIFICANTLY over the decades — the literacy rate has risen substantially since independence (from very low levels to a majority of the population now being literate), reflecting the expansion of education. However, important GAPS REMAIN: between MALES and FEMALES (female literacy still lags male literacy), between different STATES/REGIONS (e.g., Kerala has very high literacy, while some northern states lag), and between rural and urban areas. Raising literacy — especially female literacy — remains an important development goal. So literacy has risen significantly, but gaps remain. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The occupational structure of India shows that __________.
options: A large share of the workforce is still engaged in the primary sector (agriculture), though the shares of industry and services are growing
The service sector employs almost no one
solution: The OCCUPATIONAL STRUCTURE of India shows that a LARGE SHARE of the workforce is STILL ENGAGED in the PRIMARY sector — mainly AGRICULTURE (farming and allied activities) — reflecting India's still largely agrarian and developing character. However, the shares of the SECONDARY (INDUSTRY) and especially the TERTIARY (SERVICES) sectors are GROWING as the economy develops and diversifies (with services, including IT, expanding notably). The gradual shift of workers out of agriculture toward industry and services is a sign of India's economic development. So a large share is still in agriculture, but industry and services are growing. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's population, being highly diverse, includes __________.
options: Many languages, religions, ethnic groups, and cultures — making it one of the most diverse populations in the world
solution: India's POPULATION is highly DIVERSE, including MANY LANGUAGES (hundreds of languages and dialects, with 22 scheduled languages), MANY RELIGIONS (Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, and others), numerous ETHNIC groups and tribes, and a vast array of CULTURES, customs, and traditions. This makes India one of the MOST DIVERSE populations/societies in the WORLD. Managing and celebrating this diversity ('unity in diversity') is a central feature of India's demography, society, and polity. So India's population is highly diverse in language, religion, ethnicity, and culture. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India's census is conducted every __________ years.
solution: India's CENSUS — the official count of the population — is conducted every TEN YEARS (once a DECADE, a 'decennial' census). The census provides comprehensive data on population size, distribution, density, growth, and composition (age, sex, literacy, religion, occupation, etc.), which is essential for planning and administration. India's census is one of the largest such exercises in the world. So the census is conducted every ten years. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The state with the highest literacy rate in India is generally __________.
solution: KERALA generally has the HIGHEST LITERACY RATE among Indian states — it is close to universal literacy, and also has the highest female literacy. Kerala's achievements in education (and health) are often cited as a model of human development achieved through social investment despite modest income. (In contrast, some states like Bihar have had among the lowest literacy rates.) So the state with the highest literacy is Kerala. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Assertion (A): The northern plains of India are densely populated. Reason (R): The plains have fertile alluvial soil, abundant water, flat land, and a favourable climate, supporting intensive agriculture and dense settlement. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the NORTHERN PLAINS of India (the Indo-Gangetic plains) are DENSELY POPULATED — indeed, they contain India's most populous states. And the reason is (R) that the plains have FERTILE ALLUVIAL SOIL, ABUNDANT WATER (from the great rivers like the Ganga and its tributaries), FLAT LAND (easy for farming, building, and transport), and a FAVOURABLE CLIMATE — all of which support INTENSIVE AGRICULTURE and DENSE SETTLEMENT. These highly favourable conditions for livelihood and living directly explain the dense population of the plains (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The government's efforts to manage population growth in India have included __________.
options: Family planning/welfare programmes, promotion of small families, education (especially of women), and improving health care
solution: The GOVERNMENT's efforts to MANAGE POPULATION GROWTH in India have included: FAMILY PLANNING/family WELFARE programmes (promoting contraception and birth spacing); the PROMOTION of SMALL FAMILIES (through awareness and incentives); EDUCATION — especially of WOMEN (female education strongly lowers fertility); and IMPROVING HEALTH CARE (including maternal and child health, which, by reducing infant mortality, encourages smaller families). India launched one of the world's earliest official family-planning programmes. These measures, along with development and rising female literacy, have contributed to the falling birth rate. So India's efforts include family planning, small-family promotion, female education, and health care. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The concept of the 'demographic dividend' is especially relevant to India because __________.
options: India has a large and growing working-age population, which, if productively employed, can accelerate economic growth
solution: The concept of the 'DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND' is especially relevant to INDIA because India has a LARGE and GROWING WORKING-AGE POPULATION (a youthful population, with a big and rising share in the productive age group) at a time when many other countries are ageing. If this large workforce is HEALTHY, EDUCATED, SKILLED, and PRODUCTIVELY EMPLOYED, it can ACCELERATE India's ECONOMIC GROWTH (through higher output, savings, and investment) — giving India a valuable 'dividend'. Seizing this opportunity (through investment in human capital and job creation) is a key priority; failing to do so could turn the youth bulge into a liability. So the demographic dividend is relevant because India has a large working-age population that can boost growth. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The states of the Indo-Gangetic plain (like UP, Bihar, and West Bengal) are among the __________ in India.
solution: The states of the INDO-GANGETIC PLAIN — such as UTTAR PRADESH, BIHAR, and WEST BENGAL — are among the MOST POPULOUS and DENSELY POPULATED in India. The fertile, well-watered plains have supported dense agricultural populations for millennia, and these states today contain a very large share of India's total population. (Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state; Bihar and West Bengal are also among the top and are very densely settled.) So the Indo-Gangetic plain states are among the most populous and dense. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In summary, India's population is best characterised as __________.
options: Huge, diverse, unevenly distributed, still growing (though more slowly), predominantly young and rural but urbanising — a central factor in the country's development and planning
solution: In summary, India's POPULATION is best characterised as: HUGE (the world's largest); DIVERSE (in language, religion, ethnicity, and culture); UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED (dense in the plains and some states, sparse in deserts, mountains, and forests); STILL GROWING (though more SLOWLY now, as birth rates fall); predominantly YOUNG (a demographic dividend opportunity) and still largely RURAL but rapidly URBANISING. All of this makes population a CENTRAL FACTOR in the country's DEVELOPMENT and PLANNING — a source of both great challenges (resources, jobs, services) and great potential (a vast workforce and market). So India's population is huge, diverse, uneven, growing, young, and urbanising — central to its development. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The state with the LOWEST population in India is __________.
solution: SIKKIM has the LOWEST POPULATION among India's states — a small Himalayan state with a small population. (Among Union Territories, some like Lakshadweep have even smaller populations.) In contrast, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Bihar are among the MOST populous states. Knowing the least and most populous states is prelims-relevant. So the least populous state is Sikkim. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Which of the following factors leads to LOW population density in a region of India?
options: Rugged terrain, harsh climate (very dry or very cold), dense forests, and poor connectivity/infrastructure
solution: Factors that lead to LOW population DENSITY in a region of India include: RUGGED TERRAIN (high mountains, steep hills — hard to farm and settle); HARSH CLIMATE (the very DRY deserts of Rajasthan, or the very COLD high Himalayas); DENSE FORESTS (difficult to clear and inhabit, as in parts of the North-East and central India); and POOR CONNECTIVITY/infrastructure and lack of economic opportunities. These unfavourable conditions make living and livelihood difficult, so few people settle there. (Fertile plains, water, industry, and good transport, by contrast, raise density.) So low density results from rugged terrain, harsh climate, forests, and poor connectivity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Migration within India (internal migration) is important to population distribution because __________.
options: Movement of people (e.g., rural-to-urban migration for jobs) redistributes population, growing cities and industrial areas while affecting source regions
solution: INTERNAL MIGRATION (movement of people WITHIN India) is important to population DISTRIBUTION because it REDISTRIBUTES people across the country. A major stream is RURAL-to-URBAN migration — people moving from villages to CITIES and INDUSTRIAL AREAS in search of JOBS, education, and better opportunities — which GROWS the cities and urban/industrial regions while affecting the SOURCE (rural) regions (which may lose working-age people). There are also rural-to-rural, urban-to-urban, and inter-state migrations. Migration thus reshapes where India's population is concentrated over time. So internal migration redistributes population, especially through rural-to-urban movement. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): India's population growth has entered a phase of decelerating growth. Reason (R): The birth rate has been declining due to development, urbanisation, rising female education, and family planning, even as the population continues to increase in absolute terms. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India's population growth has entered a phase of DECELERATING GROWTH (the growth rate is slowing). And the reason is (R) that the BIRTH RATE has been DECLINING — due to DEVELOPMENT, URBANISATION, RISING FEMALE EDUCATION, and FAMILY PLANNING (and the higher cost of raising children) — EVEN AS the population CONTINUES to INCREASE in absolute terms (because births still exceed deaths and because of population momentum from the large young population). The fall in the birth rate is precisely what causes the growth rate to slow (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The 'child sex ratio' in India is a matter of concern because __________.
options: It has been low and declining in some areas, indicating discrimination against the girl child (son preference and sex-selective practices)
solution: The CHILD SEX RATIO in India (girls per 1,000 boys in the 0–6 age group) is a matter of CONCERN because it has been LOW and even DECLINING in some areas/states — indicating DISCRIMINATION against the GIRL CHILD, driven by SON PREFERENCE and SEX-SELECTIVE practices (including sex-selective abortion, where it occurs) and neglect of girls. A low child sex ratio is an alarming sign of gender inequality at the very start of life, prompting government campaigns (like 'Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao') and laws (banning sex determination) to address it. So the low/declining child sex ratio indicates discrimination against girls. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The distribution of population in India can be studied at various levels — national, state, district, etc. This helps in __________.
options: Understanding regional patterns and planning for the specific needs of different areas (services, resources, development)
solution: Studying the DISTRIBUTION of POPULATION in India at various LEVELS — NATIONAL, STATE, DISTRICT, and even village/city — HELPS in UNDERSTANDING REGIONAL PATTERNS (which areas are crowded or sparse, and why) and in PLANNING for the SPECIFIC NEEDS of DIFFERENT AREAS (allocating services, resources, and development efforts where people are, and addressing regional imbalances and the challenges of both crowded and sparsely populated regions). Detailed, multi-level population data are thus essential tools for effective governance and planning in a large, diverse country. So multi-level study of distribution aids understanding regional patterns and area-specific planning. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The high population density in India's river valleys and deltas is due to __________.
options: Fertile soil, abundant water, and suitability for intensive agriculture, which have supported dense settlement
solution: The HIGH population DENSITY in India's RIVER VALLEYS and DELTAS (like the Ganga plain and the deltas of the Ganga-Brahmaputra, Krishna, Godavari, and Kaveri) is due to their FERTILE (alluvial) SOIL, ABUNDANT WATER, and SUITABILITY for INTENSIVE AGRICULTURE (especially rice cultivation). These favourable conditions have SUPPORTED DENSE SETTLEMENT and large agricultural populations for a very long time. River valleys and deltas are among the most crowded parts of India (and the world). So high density in river valleys/deltas is due to fertile soil, water, and good agriculture. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rise in the proportion of the elderly in India's population in the future will require __________.
options: Increased provision for elderly care, health services, and pensions/social security
solution: As India's population AGES in the future (with rising life expectancy and falling birth rates gradually increasing the proportion of ELDERLY), it will REQUIRE INCREASED PROVISION for ELDERLY CARE, HEALTH SERVICES (for age-related needs), and PENSIONS/SOCIAL SECURITY (to support those no longer working). Although India currently has a young population (the demographic dividend), it must plan ahead for the eventual growth of its elderly population, which will bring new demands on health, care, and welfare systems. So future ageing will require more elderly care, health services, and pensions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The literacy gap between males and females in India reflects __________.
options: Historical gender inequality in access to education, which needs to be closed by promoting female education
solution: The LITERACY GAP between MALES and FEMALES in India (female literacy lagging behind male literacy) reflects HISTORICAL GENDER INEQUALITY in ACCESS to EDUCATION — girls have traditionally had fewer opportunities to attend and complete school (due to poverty, social attitudes, early marriage, domestic duties, and discrimination). This gap needs to be CLOSED by PROMOTING FEMALE EDUCATION, since educating girls and women brings wide benefits (better health, lower fertility, higher incomes, and empowerment). The gap has been narrowing over time but persists in many areas. So the male–female literacy gap reflects gender inequality in education access, to be closed by promoting female education. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'working population' in India includes __________.
options: Main workers and marginal workers (those engaged in economic activity), while the rest are non-workers (like students, homemakers, children, and the elderly not working)
solution: The 'WORKING POPULATION' in India (as classified in the census) includes those ENGAGED in ECONOMIC ACTIVITY — divided into MAIN WORKERS (who work for a major part of the year) and MARGINAL WORKERS (who work for only a part of the year). The REST are NON-WORKERS — such as STUDENTS, HOMEMAKERS, CHILDREN, dependents, and the ELDERLY who are not working. The proportion and composition of workers (and their distribution across the primary, secondary, and tertiary sectors) tell us about the economy's structure and the utilisation of the population. So the working population comprises main and marginal workers, versus non-workers. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): A large young population can be either an asset or a burden for India. Reason (R): If educated, healthy, and employed, the youth boost the economy (demographic dividend); if not, they can become a source of unemployment and unrest. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that a large YOUNG POPULATION can be EITHER an ASSET or a BURDEN for India. And the reason is (R) that IF the youth are EDUCATED, HEALTHY, and productively EMPLOYED, they BOOST the ECONOMY (realising the demographic dividend — a large, productive workforce driving growth); but IF they are NOT (left uneducated, unskilled, and jobless), they can become a source of UNEMPLOYMENT, frustration, and social UNREST (a demographic liability). Because the outcome depends entirely on how well the young are invested in and absorbed into work, the same youth bulge can be an asset or a burden (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The rapid urbanisation of India presents both opportunities and challenges. A major challenge is __________.
options: Providing adequate housing, water, sanitation, transport, and jobs in fast-growing cities, and managing slums and pollution
solution: The RAPID URBANISATION of India presents both opportunities (economic growth, jobs, services, innovation) and CHALLENGES. A MAJOR CHALLENGE is PROVIDING ADEQUATE HOUSING, WATER, SANITATION, TRANSPORT, electricity, and JOBS in FAST-GROWING CITIES that are expanding faster than infrastructure and services can keep up — leading to problems such as the growth of SLUMS, overcrowding, POLLUTION, traffic congestion, and strains on urban resources. Managing urban growth so that cities are livable, inclusive, and sustainable is a key task for India's development. So a major urbanisation challenge is providing housing, services, and jobs and managing slums/pollution. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes India's demographic situation?
options: A large, young, growing (but decelerating) population with an adverse sex ratio, rising literacy, and a shift underway from a rural-agrarian toward an urban-industrial-service society
solution: India's DEMOGRAPHIC SITUATION is correctly described as: a LARGE (world's biggest), YOUNG population; GROWING but at a DECELERATING rate (as birth rates fall); with an ADVERSE SEX RATIO (fewer females); RISING (though still uneven) LITERACY; and undergoing a gradual SHIFT from a RURAL-AGRARIAN society toward a more URBAN-INDUSTRIAL-SERVICE society (with urbanisation increasing and the workforce slowly moving out of agriculture). This dynamic, transitional demographic profile captures where India stands in its development. So option 1 correctly describes India's demographic situation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The census data on population composition help the government to __________.
options: Plan and target policies and services (education, health, jobs, welfare) according to the age, sex, literacy, and other characteristics of the population
Only count heads with no use
solution: The CENSUS DATA on POPULATION COMPOSITION HELP the government to PLAN and TARGET POLICIES and SERVICES according to the actual CHARACTERISTICS of the population. Knowing the AGE structure helps plan schools (for children), jobs (for the working-age), and pensions/healthcare (for the elderly); knowing the SEX ratio helps address gender issues; knowing LITERACY levels guides education policy; and knowing the OCCUPATIONAL and rural-urban structure informs economic and development planning. Thus detailed composition data enable evidence-based, well-targeted governance and welfare. So census composition data help plan and target policies/services to population characteristics. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall relationship between population and development in India is that __________.
options: Population is both a resource (a large workforce and market that can drive development) and a challenge (pressure on resources and services), so managing it well is key to development
Population has no link to development
A large population always guarantees development
solution: The overall RELATIONSHIP between POPULATION and DEVELOPMENT in India is that population is BOTH a RESOURCE and a CHALLENGE. As a RESOURCE, India's large population — especially its big WORKFORCE and huge MARKET — can DRIVE DEVELOPMENT (production, consumption, innovation, and a demographic dividend), if its people are educated, healthy, and employed. As a CHALLENGE, a large and growing population puts PRESSURE on RESOURCES, food, jobs, services, and the ENVIRONMENT. Therefore, MANAGING population well — investing in human capital, controlling growth, and providing for people — is KEY to turning it into an asset for development. So population is both a resource and a challenge, and managing it is key to development. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In conclusion, the study of India's population is important because __________.
options: Understanding the size, distribution, growth, and composition of its people is essential for planning India's development, welfare, and future
Only the economy matters, not people
solution: In conclusion, the STUDY of INDIA's POPULATION is IMPORTANT because UNDERSTANDING the SIZE, DISTRIBUTION, GROWTH, and COMPOSITION of its PEOPLE is ESSENTIAL for PLANNING India's DEVELOPMENT, WELFARE, and FUTURE. Since people are both the central concern and the greatest resource of the nation, knowing how many there are, where they live, how their numbers are changing, and what characteristics they have allows the government and society to provide for their needs (food, jobs, education, health, housing), to harness their potential (the demographic dividend), and to address challenges (resource pressure, inequality, ageing). So studying India's population is essential for planning its development and future. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a densely populated state due to industrial and urban development (rather than mainly agriculture)?
options: Maharashtra (with Mumbai/Pune) and the NCT of Delhi
solution: MAHARASHTRA (with the major industrial-commercial cities of MUMBAI and PUNE) and the NCT of DELHI are examples of densely populated areas whose high population owes much to INDUSTRIAL and URBAN DEVELOPMENT (jobs, industry, commerce, and services attracting people) — rather than mainly to agriculture (as in the plains). Delhi, in particular, has extremely high density as a major urban centre. This shows that economic and urban factors, not just fertile land, can produce dense populations. (The Thar Desert, Arunachal Pradesh, and Ladakh, by contrast, are sparsely populated.) So Maharashtra and Delhi are dense due to industry/urbanisation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The declining but still relatively high birth rate in India means that __________.
options: The population will continue to grow for some decades (population momentum) before eventually stabilising
The population will immediately stop growing
There will be no more births
solution: The DECLINING but still relatively HIGH birth rate in India means that the POPULATION will CONTINUE to GROW for some DECADES before eventually STABILISING. This is due to 'POPULATION MOMENTUM': because India has a large YOUNG population (many people entering their reproductive years), the number of births will remain high for a while even as the birth RATE per woman falls — so the total population keeps rising. Only after this momentum works through (and fertility settles at a low level) will the population growth level off. So India's population will keep growing for some decades due to momentum, before stabilising. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The uneven distribution of population across Indian states creates the need for __________.
options: Balanced regional development and appropriate allocation of resources and services to both densely and sparsely populated areas
solution: The UNEVEN DISTRIBUTION of population across Indian states CREATES the NEED for BALANCED REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT and the APPROPRIATE ALLOCATION of RESOURCES and SERVICES to BOTH densely and sparsely populated areas. Densely populated regions need enough services, jobs, and infrastructure to cope with their large numbers and to relieve pressure; sparsely populated and less-developed regions need development efforts, connectivity, and services to bring them into the mainstream and prevent them from being neglected. Addressing regional imbalances is thus an important goal of Indian planning. So uneven distribution creates the need for balanced regional development and resource allocation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In the final analysis, India's population is best seen as __________.
options: The nation's greatest asset and biggest responsibility — a vast human resource whose development and welfare are central to India's progress
solution: In the FINAL ANALYSIS, India's POPULATION is best seen as the NATION's GREATEST ASSET and BIGGEST RESPONSIBILITY — a VAST HUMAN RESOURCE whose DEVELOPMENT and WELFARE are CENTRAL to India's PROGRESS. Its people are the ultimate source of India's strength (labour, talent, enterprise, and a huge market) and the ultimate purpose of development (improving their lives). Realising the potential of this enormous population — by educating, keeping healthy, empowering, and employing its people, and by providing for their needs — is the key to India's future prosperity and to fulfilling the promise of its demographic dividend. So India's population is its greatest asset and responsibility, central to its progress. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The largest religious community in India is __________.
options: Hindus (the majority), followed by Muslims (the largest minority)
solution: The LARGEST religious community in India is the HINDUS, who form the MAJORITY of the population (around 80%). The largest MINORITY community is the MUSLIMS (around 14%), making India home to one of the world's largest Muslim populations. Other communities include Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, and others. India's religious composition reflects its great diversity and its secular constitutional framework. So Hindus are the majority, Muslims the largest minority. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The 'density of population' for India as a whole has __________ over the decades.
options: Increased steadily (as the total population has grown while the land area is fixed)
solution: The DENSITY of POPULATION for India as a whole has INCREASED STEADILY over the decades. Since population density = total population ÷ land area, and India's TOTAL POPULATION has GROWN enormously while its LAND AREA is FIXED, the number of persons per square kilometre has risen continuously (India now has a high average density of several hundred persons per sq km). This rising density reflects the growing pressure of population on the land. So India's population density has increased steadily over time. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The scheduled languages of India (recognised in the Constitution) number __________.
solution: The SCHEDULED LANGUAGES of India — those officially recognised in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution — number 22. These include major languages such as Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Marathi, Tamil, Urdu, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi, and others. Beyond these, India has hundreds of other languages and dialects. This linguistic multiplicity is a key aspect of India's population composition and diversity. So there are 22 scheduled languages. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Assertion (A): Population data are collected through the census in India. Reason (R): The census provides comprehensive, house-to-house counts of the population and its characteristics, forming the basis for planning and policy. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that POPULATION DATA are collected through the CENSUS in India. And the reason is (R) that the census provides COMPREHENSIVE, HOUSE-TO-HOUSE COUNTS of the POPULATION and its CHARACTERISTICS (age, sex, literacy, religion, occupation, etc.), FORMING the BASIS for PLANNING and POLICY. Because the census systematically enumerates the entire population and gathers detailed data every ten years, it is the authoritative source of population information used for governance, resource allocation, and development planning (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: A high rural population share in India indicates that __________.
options: A large part of the population still depends on agriculture and rural livelihoods, and rural development remains crucial
solution: A HIGH RURAL POPULATION share in India (a large proportion of people living in villages) INDICATES that a LARGE PART of the population still DEPENDS on AGRICULTURE and RURAL LIVELIHOODS (farming and allied activities), and that India is still largely an agrarian society (though changing). It means that RURAL DEVELOPMENT — improving agriculture, rural infrastructure, services, and non-farm rural employment — REMAINS CRUCIAL for the welfare of the majority and for the country's overall development. So a high rural share means agriculture-dependent livelihoods and the ongoing importance of rural development. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The population of India is spread across states of very different sizes and densities, which means that __________.
options: Population figures must be understood alongside area — a large-population state may or may not be densely populated depending on its size
All large states are equally dense
Population and area are the same thing
solution: The population of India is spread across states of VERY DIFFERENT SIZES and DENSITIES, which means that POPULATION FIGURES must be UNDERSTOOD ALONGSIDE AREA. A state with a LARGE POPULATION may or may not be densely populated, DEPENDING on its SIZE: for example, a large state with a large area might have moderate density, while a small state (or union territory) with a smaller population could still be very densely packed (like Delhi). Thus, to properly compare and understand states, one must consider BOTH total population AND density (population relative to area) — they are distinct measures. So population must be read together with area/density. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall study of India's population, density, growth, and composition equips planners to __________.
options: Anticipate and provide for the needs of India's people — food, jobs, education, health, housing, and services — and to harness the population as a resource for development
solution: The overall STUDY of India's POPULATION, DENSITY, GROWTH, and COMPOSITION EQUIPS PLANNERS to ANTICIPATE and PROVIDE for the NEEDS of India's people — FOOD, JOBS, EDUCATION, HEALTH care, HOUSING, water, sanitation, and other SERVICES — and to HARNESS the population as a RESOURCE for DEVELOPMENT (planning for the workforce, the demographic dividend, and human capital). By understanding how many people there are, where they live, how their numbers are changing, and what they are like, planners can design effective, forward-looking policies to improve welfare and drive progress. So studying population equips planners to meet people's needs and harness the population for development. So option 1 is correct.

stem: India, though second in area rank, holds the __________ position among countries by population.
solution: India has become the most populous country in the world (recently overtaking China), while holding only about 2.4% of the world's land area.

stem: India accounts for roughly what share of the world's population, on only about 2.4% of its land area?
solution: India holds about 17-18% of the world's population on just about 2.4% of the world's land area — reflecting heavy population pressure.

stem: The most populous state in India is:
solution: Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state in India.

stem: Population density (persons per sq km) in India is highest in states/areas like Bihar and the northern plains, and lowest in:
options: Arunachal Pradesh and the mountainous/desert states
solution: Density is highest in the fertile plains (Bihar, UP, West Bengal) and lowest in mountainous or desert states like Arunachal Pradesh.

stem: The states of the Indo-Gangetic plain (UP, Bihar, West Bengal) are among the __________ in India.
solution: The fertile Indo-Gangetic plain states (UP, Bihar, West Bengal) are among the most densely populated in India.

stem: The high population density in India's river valleys and deltas is due to:
options: fertile alluvial soil, water availability, flat land and favourable climate for agriculture
solution: River valleys and deltas have fertile soil, water, flat land and favourable climate, supporting intensive agriculture and dense settlement.

stem: Which of the following is a densely populated state due mainly to industrial and urban development (rather than agriculture)?
options: Maharashtra (with Mumbai) or West Bengal (with Kolkata)
solution: States like Maharashtra (Mumbai) and West Bengal (Kolkata) have high density partly due to industrial and urban development.

stem: India's population 'explosion' (very rapid growth) occurred especially after:
solution: India's rapid population growth (the population explosion) occurred especially after 1951, as death rates fell sharply.

stem: The main reason for India's rapid population growth in the 20th century was:
options: a sharp decline in the death rate (due to better healthcare, food and sanitation) while birth rates stayed high
solution: Rapid growth resulted mainly from a sharp fall in death rates (better healthcare, food, sanitation) while birth rates remained high.

stem: In recent decades, India's population growth RATE has:
options: begun to decline/slow (though the population keeps growing in absolute numbers)
solution: India's population growth rate has begun to decline in recent decades, though the population continues to increase in absolute numbers.

stem: The sex ratio in India (females per 1000 males) has historically been:
solution: India's sex ratio has historically been unfavourable (fewer females per 1000 males), reflecting gender bias.

stem: The 'child sex ratio' in India is a matter of concern because:
options: it has declined, indicating gender bias against the girl child (e.g., sex-selective practices)
solution: The declining child sex ratio indicates gender bias against the girl child (sex-selective abortion, neglect), a serious concern.

stem: India's age structure shows that a large proportion of its population is:
options: young (in the working and pre-working age groups)
solution: India has a youthful age structure, with a large proportion of young people — the basis of its demographic dividend potential.

stem: The concept of the 'demographic dividend' is especially relevant to India because:
options: it has a large and growing working-age population that, if developed and employed, can boost the economy
solution: India's large young/working-age population offers a demographic dividend if it is educated, skilled, healthy and employed.

stem: The majority of India's population still lives in:
options: rural (village) areas, though urbanisation is increasing
solution: The majority of India's population still lives in rural areas, though the level of urbanisation is rising.

stem: A high rural population share in India indicates that:
options: a large part of the population still depends on agriculture and rural livelihoods
solution: A high rural share indicates that a large part of the population still depends on agriculture and rural livelihoods.

stem: The occupational structure of India shows that:
options: a large share of the workforce is still engaged in agriculture (the primary sector)
solution: India's occupational structure shows a large share of the workforce still engaged in agriculture (the primary sector), though this is slowly declining.

stem: Literacy in India has __________ over the decades, though gaps remain.
solution: Literacy in India has risen substantially over the decades, though gaps remain (by gender, region, rural-urban).

stem: The state with the highest literacy rate in India is generally:
solution: Kerala generally has the highest literacy rate among Indian states.

stem: The literacy gap between males and females in India reflects:
options: persisting gender disparities in access to education
solution: The male-female literacy gap reflects persisting gender disparities in access to education, though the gap is narrowing.

stem: The largest religious community in India is:
solution: Hindus form the largest religious community in India.

stem: The scheduled languages of India, recognised in the Constitution, number:
solution: There are 22 scheduled languages recognised in the Constitution of India.

stem: India's population, being highly diverse, includes:
options: many religions, languages, castes and ethnic groups
solution: India's population is highly diverse, comprising many religions, languages, castes and ethnic groups.

stem: Migration within India (internal migration) is important to population distribution because it:
options: redistributes population (e.g., rural-to-urban migration reshapes where people live)
solution: Internal migration (especially rural-to-urban) redistributes population, reshaping the distribution across regions and cities.

stem: The government's efforts to manage population growth in India have included:
options: family planning/welfare programmes and promoting education and awareness
solution: India has pursued family planning/welfare programmes and promoted education and awareness to manage population growth.

stem: The rise in the proportion of the elderly in India's future population will require:
options: greater provision of healthcare, pensions and elderly care
solution: A rising elderly proportion will require greater provision of healthcare, pensions and elderly-care services.

stem: The rapid urbanisation of India presents challenges such as:
options: pressure on housing, infrastructure, services, and the growth of slums and pollution
solution: Rapid urbanisation strains housing, infrastructure and services and can lead to slums and pollution — major challenges.

stem: The state with the LOWEST population in India is generally:
solution: Sikkim is generally the least populous state in India.

stem: The uneven distribution of population across Indian states creates the need for:
options: region-specific planning and balanced development to address disparities
solution: Uneven distribution requires region-specific planning and balanced development to address disparities in resources and services.

stem: The declining but still relatively high birth rate in India means that:
options: the population continues to grow in absolute numbers for now, though the growth rate is slowing
solution: A declining but still relatively high birth rate means the population keeps growing in absolute terms, even as the growth rate slows.

stem: The study of India's population at national, state and district levels helps in:
options: planning for resources, services and development at the appropriate scale
solution: Studying population at various levels helps in planning for resources, services and development at the appropriate scale.

stem: The census data on population composition help the government to:
options: plan for education, health, employment and welfare according to the population's structure
solution: Census data on composition help the government plan for education, health, employment and welfare according to the population's structure.

stem: The overall relationship between population and development in India is that:
options: population is both a resource (workforce) and a challenge (pressure on resources), so development must harness the former and manage the latter
solution: India's population is both a resource (a large workforce) and a challenge (pressure on resources); development must harness the potential and manage the pressures.

stem: Assertion (A): India faces the challenge of a large and growing population. Reason (R): A large population puts pressure on resources, food, jobs, services and the environment, requiring careful planning. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: a large, growing population strains resources, food, jobs, services and the environment, requiring careful planning.

stem: Assertion (A): The northern plains of India are densely populated. Reason (R): The plains have fertile alluvial soil, abundant water, flat land and a favourable climate, supporting intensive agriculture and dense settlement. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: the plains' fertile soil, water, flat land and favourable climate support dense settlement.

stem: Assertion (A): India's population growth has entered a phase of decelerating growth. Reason (R): The birth rate has been declining due to development, urbanisation, rising female education and family planning, even as the population still increases. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: falling birth rates (from development, urbanisation, female education, family planning) have decelerated the growth rate.

stem: Assertion (A): A large young population can be either an asset or a burden for India. Reason (R): If educated, healthy and employed, the youth boost the economy (demographic dividend); if not, they can become a source of unemployment and unrest. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: whether the youth are an asset or a burden depends on whether they are educated, healthy and employed.

stem: The 'working population' in India includes:
options: those in the working-age group who are engaged in or available for economic activity
solution: The working population includes those in the working-age group who are engaged in, or available for, economic activity.

stem: In conclusion, the study of India's population is important because it:
options: informs planning for development, resources, services and welfare for a huge and diverse population
solution: Studying India's population informs planning for development, resources, services and welfare for its huge and diverse population.

stem: The overall study of India's population equips planners to:
options: allocate resources, plan services and design policies suited to the population's size, distribution and structure
solution: It equips planners to allocate resources, plan services and design policies suited to the population's size, distribution and structure.

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter 'Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition' (India)?
options: India has a huge, unevenly distributed, young and diverse population that is growing (though decelerating); understanding its distribution, density, growth and composition is essential for planning and development
solution: The chapter concludes that India has a huge, unevenly distributed, young and diverse population that is growing (though decelerating), and that understanding its distribution, density, growth and composition is essential for planning and development.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition' (India) is that:
options: India's population is small and evenly distributed

India is the world's MOST POPULOUS country, with a large and (until recently rapidly) growing population that is very UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED — densely settled in the fertile northern plains and states like Kerala, and sparse in deserts, mountains, and forests — with density and distribution shaped by physical and human factors; population growth was slow before 1921 (the 'Great Divide'), then rapid (a 'population explosion') due to falling death rates with high birth rates, but the growth rate has begun to slow in recent decades as birth rates fall; and India's population COMPOSITION features a largely rural but rapidly urbanising society, a young/working-age age structure (a demographic dividend opportunity), an adverse sex ratio, rising but uneven literacy, a workforce still largely in agriculture, and enormous linguistic, religious, and cultural diversity — making population a central factor in India's development
solution: The chapter's overall message is that INDIA is the world's MOST POPULOUS country, with a LARGE and (until recently rapidly) GROWING population that is very UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED across the country. Population is DENSELY concentrated in the fertile NORTHERN PLAINS (the most populous states — Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal — and high-density states like Kerala and Delhi) and SPARSE in the DESERTS, high MOUNTAINS, and dense FORESTS. Both DISTRIBUTION and DENSITY are shaped by PHYSICAL factors (relief, climate, water, soil) and HUMAN factors (agriculture, industry, urbanisation, transport). In terms of GROWTH, India's population grew SLOWLY and fluctuated BEFORE 1921 (the 'YEAR of the GREAT DIVIDE'), then grew RAPIDLY (a 'POPULATION EXPLOSION') from 1921 onward — mainly because DEATH RATES FELL sharply (better health, food, and control of famines/epidemics) while BIRTH RATES REMAINED HIGH — but in RECENT DECADES the growth RATE has begun to SLOW as birth rates fall (though the total population still rises). India's population COMPOSITION features: a still largely RURAL but rapidly URBANISING society; a YOUNG, working-age AGE STRUCTURE offering a DEMOGRAPHIC DIVIDEND opportunity; an ADVERSE SEX RATIO (fewer females, reflecting gender discrimination); RISING but UNEVEN LITERACY (with male–female and regional gaps); an OCCUPATIONAL structure still dominated by AGRICULTURE but with growing industry and services; and ENORMOUS LINGUISTIC, RELIGIOUS, ethnic, and cultural DIVERSITY. All this makes population a central factor in India's development, presenting both challenges (pressure on resources and services) and opportunities (a vast workforce). So the overall message is option 2.
